segments.text: "Name" — and a word that shows off a famous Kannada sound-law.
(Skim if you read Kannada.) ಹ (ha) + ೆ (the e-sign) becomes ಹೆ (he); ಸ (sa); ರು (ru). Read ಹೆ, ಸ, ರು becomes hesaru.

ಹೆಸರು (hesaru, "name") is native Dravidian, from Proto-Dravidian pesar — and it hides a famous Kannada sound-law: an old initial p became h. So pesar becomes hesar becomes hesaru. That makes it a cousin of Tamil peyar (same root; Tamil kept the p, Kannada softened it to h) — and, like peyar, not related to Sanskrit nāma (Hindi nām, English name).
Across the family: Kannada hesaru, Tamil peyar, Telugu pēru, Malayalam pēr — one Dravidian word; only Hindi nām / English name are Indo-European.

blocks.title: Across the family — the same idea, five ways

utterances: Language: Kannada. "Name": ಹೆಸರು hesaru. Source: Dravidian pesar (p becomes h).
Language: Tamil. "Name": peyar. Source: the same Dravidian root (kept p).
Language: Telugu. "Name": pēru. Source: the same Dravidian root.
Language: Malayalam. "Name": pēr. Source: the same Dravidian root.

segments.text: The p becomes h shift is why hesaru looks unlike its sisters — but it is the same word.

segments.text: "My" — native Dravidian, with no European cousin.
(Skim if you read Kannada.) ನ (na) + the conjunct ನ್ನ (nna) becomes nanna — a doubled, held nn.

ನನ್ನ (nanna) means "my." It belongs to Kannada's native Dravidian first-person family, not to the Indo-European family behind English I/my. The stem underneath is Dravidian nān — the same one behind Tamil nāṉ / eṉ. You will meet the related word for "I" in its own lesson; today you only need nanna.
What does ನನ್ನ (nanna) mean? ("My.") Is it native Dravidian or an Indo-European loan? (Native Dravidian.)

lessons.title: ನನ್ನ ಹೆಸರು … (nanna hesaru …) — "my name is…," with no "is"

segments.text: Assemble the two atoms — and notice, as in Tamil, no word for "is."

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The phrase, assembled

segments.text: nanna (my) + hesaru (name) + your name.
ನನ್ನ ಹೆಸರು … (nanna hesaru …) = "my name …" becomes "my name is…"
Nanna hesaru Arun. becomes "My name is Arun."
There is no verb. Kannada sets "my name" beside "Arun" and lets the "is" be understood — the zero copula of the Dravidian family (just like Tamil). Nanna hesaru Arun = literally "my name Arun."
Give your name in Kannada. (Nanna hesaru ….) What does Kannada leave out that English needs? (The verb "is" — zero copula.)

segments.text: "You" — and Kannada makes respect the same way Tamil and French do.
(Skim if you read Kannada.) ನೀ (nī) + ನು (nu) becomes nīnu; ನೀ + ವು (vu) becomes nīvu.
ನೀನು (nīnu, familiar "you") from Proto-Dravidian nīn — the same native root as Tamil nī. ನೀವು (nīvu) is the respectful/plural "you."

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: respect by the plural

segments.text: nīnu (familiar) vs. nīvu (respectful, and literally plural) — the same politeness-by-plural as Tamil nīṅgaḷ and French vous: one respected person addressed as "you all." For a first meeting, nīvu.
How does Kannada make "you" respectful, and which languages use the same trick? (By the plural — nīvu; Tamil nīṅgaḷ, French vous.)

segments.text: The last piece of the question: "what."
(Skim if you read Kannada.) ಏ (independent long ē, word-initial) + ನು (nu) becomes ēnu.

ಏನು (ēnu, "what") is native Dravidian, on the interrogative stem yā- / e- — the same Dravidian question-root as Tamil eṉṉa, heading Kannada's question family: ēnu (what), yāru (who), elli (where), yāke (why).

segments.text: What Dravidian stem heads ಏನು (ēnu) and Kannada's other question-words? (yā-/e-, the same as Tamil eṉṉa.)

lessons.title: ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹೆಸರು ಏನು? (nimma hesaru ēnu?) — "what's your name?"

segments.text: Assemble the question — your + name + what — still no "is."

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The phrase, assembled

segments.text: ನಿಮ್ಮ (nimma, "your") = the possessive of nīvu ("you," respectful).
ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹೆಸರು ಏನು? (nimma hesaru ēnu?) = literally "your name what?" = "what's your name?"
Three words, no verb — the zero copula holds for questions too.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: answer, and the familiar version

segments.text: Answer with the sentence you built: Nanna hesaru Arun. The familiar "your" is ninna (from nīnu): ninna hesaru ēnu?

segments.text: One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is a vowel sign. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it with e. Replaces, not adds — the a is gone.
You already say these, and every one of them has ◌ೆ somewhere inside it:
ಹೆಸರು hesaru — name.
ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹೆಸರು ಏನು? nimma hesaru ēnu? — what is your name?

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The phrase

segments.text: The full form is ನಿಮ್ಮನ್ನು ಭೇಟಿಯಾಗಿ ಸಂತೋಷ (nimmannu bhēṭiyāgi santōṣa) — "having met you, joy."

ಸಂತೋಷ (santōṣa, "joy, contentment") is Sanskrit — sam- ("fully") + toṣa ("satisfaction") — not native. Where Tamil reaches for its home-grown magiḻcci, Kannada uses a Sanskrit word even for "pleased." The same split you saw over "hello" (namaskāra) and "thanks" (dhanyavāda) runs right through the introductions: Kannada borrows, Tamil keeps its own.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The dialogue

utterances: ನನ್ನ ಹೆಸರು ಮೀರಾ. (nanna hesaru Mira) means My name is Mira.
ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹೆಸರು ಏನು? (nimma hesaru ēnu?) (nimma hesaru ēnu) means What's your name?
ನನ್ನ ಹೆಸರು ಅರುಣ್. (nanna hesaru Arun) means My name is Arun.
ಸಂತೋಷ. (santōṣa) means Pleased to meet you.

segments.text: Every atom traced:
hesaru from Dravidian pesar (p becomes h; cousin of Tamil peyar, not name).
nanna from nānu ("I").
ēnu from Dravidian question-stem yā-/e-.
santōṣa from Sanskrit (Kannada borrows even for "pleased"; Tamil keeps native magiḻcci).
The Kannada habit: the zero copula (no "is"). And the family thread — native Dravidian grammar words, a Sanskrit word for "pleased."
